lesson.title: Wiring That Learns: Long-Term Potentiation
lesson.summary: Long-term potentiation is the lasting strengthening of the connection between two neurons that occurs when they are activated together repeatedly, and it is the leading biological mechanism thought to underlie learning and memory.
lesson.body:
Long-term potentiation, often abbreviated LTP, is a lasting increase in the strength of the connection between two neurons that follows repeated or intense stimulation of the synapse between them. In simple terms, when one neuron repeatedly helps activate another, the synapse connecting them becomes more efficient, so the first neuron can trigger the second one more easily in the future. This echoes a principle proposed by psychologist Donald Hebb before the underlying biology was understood: neurons that fire together tend to wire together. LTP was first identified in the hippocampus, and remains the most thoroughly studied cellular mechanism thought to underlie learning and the storage of new memories.

The biological basis of LTP is a direct application of ordinary neural transmission, pushed into a lasting change. When a presynaptic neuron fires, it releases a neurotransmitter, commonly glutamate, which crosses the synapse and binds to receptors on the receiving, postsynaptic neuron. Under repeated or strong stimulation, this binding activates a receptor type known as the NMDA receptor, allowing calcium to flow into the postsynaptic neuron. That calcium influx sets off a cascade inside the cell that increases the number and sensitivity of a different receptor type, AMPA receptors, on the postsynaptic membrane. The result is that the very same amount of neurotransmitter released in the future produces a stronger response than it used to, because the receiving neuron has become more sensitive to it.

LTP is closely tied to the hippocampus, the structure most central to forming new explicit memories. Because the hippocampal circuits that support new learning are also where LTP has been most extensively documented, LTP is treated as the best-supported cellular candidate for how the hippocampus encodes new experiences at the level of individual synapses. This gives psychologists a bridge between a molecular process and a psychological one, connecting the biology of neural transmission to the mental experience of learning something new.

As a simplified illustration, imagine repeatedly encountering a particular scent in a particular location, such as the smell of a bakery you pass every morning on a familiar street corner. Each time the smell and the location are experienced together, the neural pathways connecting the brain's representation of that scent to its representation of that location get activated together, and LTP strengthens the synapses along that shared pathway. Eventually, encountering the smell alone, somewhere else entirely, may be enough to bring the street corner to mind, because the connection between them has been potentiated. In reality, an actual memory like this is distributed across vast networks of neurons rather than just two, but the underlying logic scales up from this same basic synaptic principle.

It is worth remembering that LTP is not memory itself, but a cellular mechanism thought to support memory formation at a larger scale. A single potentiated synapse does not constitute a memory any more than a single brick constitutes a building; memories are believed to be patterns of synaptic change distributed across many neurons and circuits. Support for the link between LTP and actual learning comes partly from research showing that drugs which block NMDA receptors, and thereby prevent LTP, also impair the ability to learn new hippocampus-dependent tasks, which is one reason psychologists and neuroscientists treat LTP as a genuine biological foundation for memory rather than just a laboratory curiosity.
